title: Eikev: open the heart (Deuteronomy 10:16)
hook: "circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no more stiffnecked"

segments.voice: Yesterday, the plainest question in the book: what does God require? Your line was what is asked is simple. Did you do your one simple thing? Today, a startling picture of a closed heart. Day four hundred ninety-five.

Chapter ten opens in the aftermath of the golden calf. Moses has just recalled the first tablets, thrown down and broken before the people's eyes. Then God tells him: carve two new tablets like the first, and come back up. He does. And the rabbis add a detail the Torah only hints at. In the Talmud they teach that the broken pieces weren't thrown away. They were placed in the ark, beside the whole tablets. A few verses later, Moses tells the people what has to change in them so it doesn't happen again.
screen: `THE TABLETS SHATTERED.` → `CARVE TWO NEW ONES.` → `THE BROKEN PIECES KEPT.`

segments.voice: In the old Jewish translation: "Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no more stiffnecked." It's a jarring image, and it's meant to be. The Hebrew word is orlah, and readers hear in it a covering, something that closes over and blocks. The Bible uses the same root for other blocked organs. Back in Exodus, Moses called himself a man of uncircumcised lips, his mouth closed, he felt, to speech. The prophet Jeremiah speaks of ears that are uncircumcised, that can't hear. So an uncircumcised heart is a heart with a layer over it. It knows things, but they don't get in. Then the second half: be no more stiffnecked. The picture, as some readers take it, comes from the farm: an ox that stiffens its neck won't turn where the driver leads. And it echoes what God called the people at the golden calf: a stiffnecked people. So Moses is naming the old problem in two pictures. A covered heart doesn't let anything in. A stiff neck won't turn toward anything. Notice who's asked to do the opening. Here, it's the people: you circumcise your heart. Later in Deuteronomy, in chapter thirty, the same image comes back, and this time it's God who promises to do it for them. Commentators hold both: the opening is your work, and it's also a gift. The broken tablets in the ark make the same point. What cracked can be carried. A heart can be opened again.
screen: `ORLAH: A COVERING.` · `UNCIRCUMCISED LIPS, EARS, HEARTS.` · `A STIFF NECK WON'T TURN.` · `YOUR WORK, AND A GIFT.` · then, large: `OPEN THE HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: soften toward one person. Settle, and breathe. Let your shoulders drop, and notice your neck, the actual muscles. Is it stiff? Let it loosen a little. Now bring to mind one person you've closed over. Someone you've stopped listening to, or turned away from. You don't have to forgive anything. Just notice the layer. What is one true thing about them that you've stopped letting in? Hold it for a few breaths, and let your neck turn toward them, just slightly. The bell holds the time.
Eikev. Because, and heel. The portion where new tablets are carved, the broken ones kept, and a covered heart is told to open.
Your line: open the heart. Today, with the person you thought of, listen for one minute without preparing your answer. Day four hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: Some Jewish teachers read this verse together with Deuteronomy 30:6 and the Talmud's teaching that the broken tablets were kept in the ark, as images of repentance, especially in the weeks leading up to the High Holy Days.

myth: the word orlah in this verse is used only for the body
the Bible also speaks of uncircumcised lips and ears: blocked, closed.
stiffnecked is the word used about the golden calf
God calls the people stiffnecked there, and Moses echoes it.
in chapter thirty, God promises to do the opening
the same image returns, as a promise.

fork.setup: you're Moses. the first tablets lie shattered after the golden calf. what does God tell you to do?
options: carve two new tablets like the first, and come back up.
fork.reveal: he carves new tablets. and the Talmud says the broken pieces were kept in the ark beside the whole ones.

original.note: Hebrew: the foreskin, the covering, of your heart. orlah is also used of lips and ears that are closed.

trapdoor: what you thought: a strange bodily metaphor.
what it means: a heart with a layer over it, that knows but doesn't let things in, and a neck too stiff to turn.
what a scholar hears: orlah also marks Moses' lips (Exodus 6:12) and closed ears (Jeremiah 6:10); Deuteronomy 30:6 makes the opening God's promise.

sources.quoted: Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no more stiffnecked.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): chapter 10 doesn't open on 'the worst day' (superlative cut; it opens with the second tablets after the calf in ch. 9); the Talmud says the broken tablets were placed in the ark, so 'carried together through the wilderness' was cut; 'the Torah uses the same word' fixed to 'the Bible uses the same root' since Jeremiah is cited; 'exact word' softened to 'echoes'; ox image framed as a reading.
Deuteronomy 10:16 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; verify.
The broken tablets kept in the ark: Berakhot 8b and Bava Batra 14b (also Menachot 99a); confirm folios.
Exodus 6:12 'uncircumcised lips' and Jeremiah 6:10 'their ear is uncircumcised' paraphrased; verify references.
Day 482 also used Moses' trouble with speech; here it appears only as an echo of the word orlah.
